data_section_full_text:
4. Sample selection


Our fraud sample only includes firms that fraudulently overstated annual earnings
(i.e., the firm misstated at least one 10-K filing). While there are other types of
fraud, overstatement of earnings is the most common type of fraud and is of fundamental concern to investors, auditors, regulators, and other users of financial
statements. We did not include frauds that misstated quarterly data because the
earnings management models in our study are designed to detect earnings management of annual data. We also limited our sample to firms for which we had access


CAR Vol. 25 No. 2 (Summer 2008)

Discretionary Accrual Models and Fraudulent and Restated Earnings 507

to the original 10-K filing and subsequent filings of restated data (i.e., 10-K/A’s,
8-K’s, etc.). We did this for two reasons. First, it was necessary to access the subsequent filing to identify the size of the restatement. Second, our primary data source
was COMPUSTAT. We found that COMPUSTAT does not consistently report
restatement data. It appears that if the restated data are available when COMPUSTAT
enters the data in its database, the restated data are entered and the fraudulent
numbers are discarded. It does not appear that COMPUSTAT changes data upon
restatements several years after the original data are entered in its database. Therefore, we compared COMPUSTAT data with the original 10-K filing to verify that
the data in COMPUSTAT are the fraudulently reported numbers and not the
restated data. We found that COMPUSTAT reports restated data for 19 of the 118
fraud firm-years in our fraud sample. We hand-collect the original fraudulent data
for those 19 firm-years. SEC filings are available on Electronic Data Gathering
Analysis and Retrieval System (EDGAR) beginning in 1994. SEC filings for
selected companies are available on Lexis/Nexis for years prior to 1994, and we
were able to locate data for several firms prior to 1994.

We identified our fraud sample from three sources. First, Committee of Sponsoring Organizations (COSO) published a report “Fraudulent Financial Reporting:
1987–1997 — An Analysis of U.S. Public Companies” (Beasley, Carcello, and
Hermanson 1999). The COSO study investigated frauds that were identified in
SEC Accounting and Auditing Enforcement Releases ( AAER s) issued during the
period 1987–1997. <sup>3</sup> COSO identifies 204 fraud firms. Second, we performed our
own search of AAER s issued from 1998 to 2004. We used “fraud” as a search term
and identified an additional 240 fraud firms. Third, we identified another 6 firms by
searching the popular press and the AAA (American Accounting Association)
monograph on litigation involving Big 4 auditors and their predecessor firms. We
excluded firms from our sample for one or more of the following reasons: did not
misreport at least one 10-K (e.g., fraudulent reported quarterly data); nonfinancial
frauds (e.g., insider trading, omitted disclosures); did not manage earnings (e.g.,
reported sales on a gross rather than a net basis, which increased sales and cost of
sales by the same amount); unable to locate company data (e.g., small firms or
foreign companies); or the firm did not have enough data available to compute discretionary accruals (e.g., firm committed fraud in an initial public offering (IPO)
and did not report a sufficient amount of data in prior years or the company was a
financial services firm). Our final fraud sample consists of 118 firms. Table 1 summarizes our sample selection procedure. Several of the firms misreported in more
than one year. Our sample includes a total of 188 firm-years that were fraudulently
reported. Since the data requirements vary across the discretionary accrual measures, the total number of fraud observations available to estimate (9) ranges from
146 to 188 depending on the discretionary measure examined. Similarly, the number
of observations for which the magnitude of the fraud is available to estimate (10)
ranges from 118 to 142.
